units.name: Newtonian Mechanics & Kinematics
units.description: Classical mechanics: Inertia, Newton's 3 laws, gravitation in vacuum, and projectile acceleration.

concepts.name: Newton's 1st Law (Inertia)
concepts.definition: An object in motion continues at constant velocity unless acted upon by a net external force (\Sigma F = 0 \iff a = 0). No force is required to sustain motion.

concepts.name: Freefall in Vacuum
concepts.definition: In vacuum, all masses fall with identical acceleration g = 9.8 m/s^2 independent of mass, as gravitational force and inertial resistance scale equally.

concepts.name: Instantaneous Acceleration
concepts.definition: Acceleration is the time rate of change of velocity (a = dv/dt). An object can have zero instantaneous velocity and non-zero acceleration simultaneously.

concepts.name: Newton's 2nd Law (F = ma)
concepts.definition: Net external force produces proportional acceleration (\Sigma F = m * a). Net force causes change in velocity, never constant velocity.

misconception_library.name: Force Needed to Sustain Motion
misconception_library.description: Believing constant velocity requires a continuous forward pushing force.
misconception_library.counter_example: Voyager 1 deep space probe cruising at 38,000 mph with engines completely powered off.
scaffold_hints: What does Newton's First Law state about an object when the net external force is zero?
If friction and air resistance are zero, what force is needed to keep an object sliding?
Distinguish between what is required to change motion (acceleration) vs what happens with no force (constant velocity).

misconception_library.name: Heavier Objects Accelerate Faster in Vacuum
misconception_library.description: Confusing greater gravitational force (F=mg) with greater acceleration (a=g).
misconception_library.counter_example: Apollo 15 astronaut dropping a heavy hammer and a light feather simultaneously on the Moon.
scaffold_hints: Earth pulls a 10kg mass with 10x more force than a 1kg mass. But according to F=ma, what does mass also resist?
Calculate acceleration: a = F_net / m. Substitute F_net = m*g. What happens to mass m in the equation?
Greater gravitational pull is exactly balanced by greater inertia (resistance to acceleration).

misconception_library.name: Zero Acceleration at Vertical Peak
misconception_library.description: Believing that because velocity is temporarily 0 at the peak, acceleration must also be 0.
misconception_library.counter_example: If acceleration were 0 at the peak, the ball would freeze and float in the air permanently!
scaffold_hints: What force is still pulling downwards on the ball when it reaches the highest point?
Acceleration is the rate of change of velocity. Is velocity staying at zero, or changing direction?
Gravity continues to act downwards at g = 9.8 m/s^2 even at the momentary turning point.

diagnostic_challenges.title: The Frictionless Ice Puck Paradox
diagnostic_challenges.prompt: A hockey puck is gliding across a completely frictionless ice rink at a constant velocity of 12 m/s. A student asserts: 'There must be a continuous forward force of 12 N pushing the puck to sustain its 12 m/s speed.' Explain why this reasoning is correct or flawed, and identify the net force acting on the puck.
diagnostic_challenges.ground_truth_concept: Net force is 0 N because constant velocity requires zero net force under Newton's 1st law.
diagnostic_challenges.transfer_question: A space probe drifts through deep space far from any celestial body at 5,000 m/s with all thrusters off. Does it slow down, speed up, or maintain speed? Explain the net force.

diagnostic_challenges.title: Bowling Ball vs Wooden Ball in Vacuum
diagnostic_challenges.prompt: A 10 kg bowling ball and a 1 kg wooden sphere are dropped simultaneously from a height of 20 meters inside a vacuum chamber. Which object reaches the floor first, and why? Explain using Newton's Second Law and gravitational force.
diagnostic_challenges.ground_truth_concept: Both reach the floor at the exact same instant because acceleration a = F/m = (mg)/m = g, making acceleration independent of mass.
diagnostic_challenges.transfer_question: On the Moon (no atmosphere), an astronaut drops a 2 kg rock and a 0.05 kg feather from 2 meters. Which strikes the lunar soil first and why?

diagnostic_challenges.title: Instantaneous Acceleration at the Peak
diagnostic_challenges.prompt: A tennis ball is thrown vertically upwards into the air. At the highest point of its flight, its instantaneous velocity is 0 m/s. What is the acceleration of the ball at this exact instant? Justify your answer using forces.
diagnostic_challenges.ground_truth_concept: Acceleration is 9.8 m/s^2 downwards because gravity is the only force acting on the ball.
diagnostic_challenges.transfer_question: A pendulum swings to its highest turning point where it momentarily comes to rest before swinging back. Is its acceleration at this turning point zero or non-zero? Explain why.

units.name: Algorithms & Recursion (Computer Science)
units.description: Recursive call stacks, base case termination, divide & conquer, and time complexity bounds.

concepts.name: Recursive Call Stack & Memory Frames
concepts.definition: Each recursive invocation allocates a new stack frame containing local variables and return address. When a base case returns, execution unwinds through parent frames in LIFO order.

concepts.name: Base Case Guard & Unwinding
concepts.definition: A base case halts further recursive branching and initiates stack unwinding. Returning in a base case only returns to the immediate caller frame, not the root.

misconception_library.name: Base Case Return Exits Entire Program
misconception_library.description: Believing that returning a value from a recursive base case immediately exits the entire algorithm without executing remaining statements in parent frames.
misconception_library.counter_example: A Russian nesting doll: opening the smallest inner doll doesn't destroy all outer dolls; you must close each outer doll one by one on the way back out!
scaffold_hints: When function call f(1) returns, where does its returned value go?
Look at the call stack: f(3) called f(2), which called f(1). When f(1) finishes, which frame resumes execution?
Remember: return hands the value back to the caller frame on top of the call stack.

diagnostic_challenges.title: Recursive Stack Unwinding Mechanics
diagnostic_challenges.prompt: Consider a recursive function `def sum_to_n(n): if n == 1: return 1; return n + sum_to_n(n-1)`. A candidate claims: 'When n==1 triggers return 1, the function terminates and immediately outputs 1 to the user.' Explain why this reasoning is incorrect and trace how stack unwinding computes the answer for n=3.
diagnostic_challenges.ground_truth_concept: The base case returns 1 to the caller frame sum_to_n(2), which evaluates 2+1=3, which returns to sum_to_n(3), which evaluates 3+3=6.
diagnostic_challenges.transfer_question: In a recursive tree traversal `def count_nodes(root): if not root: return 0; return 1 + count_nodes(root.left) + count_nodes(root.right)`, what happens when `root.left` reaches `None` and returns 0?
